samples.summary: Attacker-influenced document content can permanently drop the DNS-rebinding address pin for the rest of an export when an egress proxy is configured, re-opening SSRF-by-rebinding through the proxy's network
samples.evidence: `planHop`'s doc comment asserts "The fallback is not attacker-triggerable: whether the proxy accepts an address literal is a property of the environment, not of the document." That is not what the code keys on. The retry branch (image-fetcher.ts:800-812) fires on ANY `SystemError` with `code === 'NETWORK_ERROR'` raised while `plan.pinnedThroughProxy` is true, and `rawRequest` (line 662-670) converts *every* thrown transport cause into exactly that — proxy CONNECT refusal, origin TCP reset, TLS handshake failure, unreachable approved address. All of those are choosable by whoever authored the document `src` (they pick the host, its DNS answers, and its TLS/TCP behaviour). On the first such failure the code sets the fetcher-scoped `pinThroughProxy = false` (line 808) and re-plans with `planHop(target, addresses, false)`, which returns a bare `ProxyAgent` with the original *name* — so the proxy now resolves the host itself for that hop and for every remaining image and redirect hop in the export. Attack: document image #1 = `http://reset.attacker.test/a.png` (gate-approved public A record, origin RSTs or serves a bad cert) → pin dropped for the run; image #2 = `http://rebind.attacker.test/b.png` served by a 0-TTL nameserver that answers the CLI's gate lookup with a public address and the proxy's lookup with `10.0.0.5`/`169.254.169.254` → the proxy fetches the internal resource and the bytes are embedded in the PDF/DOCX/PPTX the victim opens. The gate cannot stop this: it resolved a different, earlier answer. The residual risk is documented for the *proxy-refuses-literal* case only, and the operator warning is emitted once, so a document-triggered drop is indistinguishable from an environmental one.

samples.summary: The new cross-site `?mode=cli` refusal cannot fire on the attack path it is documented as closing — `CliLoginConfirmMiddleware` short-circuits that navigation before the guard runs
samples.evidence: `AuthModule.configure` wires `CliLoginConfirmMiddleware` on `GET auth/github` (packages/backend/src/auth/auth.module.ts:47-48), and the middleware returns the confirmation page with `res.status(200).send(...)` without calling `next()` whenever `mode === 'cli'` and `parseCliPort` succeeds (cli-login-confirm.middleware.ts:106-113). The threat the new check names — "a hostile page navigating the victim's browser into a CLI login it chose the parameters of" — is exactly such a request (mode=cli plus an attacker-chosen port), so it terminates at the middleware and `GitHubAuthGuard.canActivate` (and therefore `assertCliStartNotCrossSite`, line 113) never executes for it. The only requests that do reach the check are the confirmation-page Continue click (relative link on the backend origin ⇒ always `same-origin`/`same-site`) and `mode=cli` starts with a missing/invalid `port`, which the CLI branch already ignores. Net effect of the control on the named attack: none; the confirm cookie is still the whole defense. This matters because `docs/design/rest-api.md` and `docs/design/backend.md` now credit the header check as the mitigation for that row of the risk table, so the flow reads as doubly covered when it is singly covered.

samples.summary: `parseFetchSite` fails OPEN on an ambiguous `Sec-Fetch-Site`: it takes the first token, so `same-origin, cross-site` is served
samples.evidence: `first.split(',')[0]` (line 60) keeps only the leading token of a duplicated or comma-folded header, and duplicated request headers are exactly what Node/express hands back joined with `, `. A hop (or anything else able to prepend a value) that yields `Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin, cross-site` is therefore accepted by `ALLOWED_FETCH_SITES`, while the mirror-image `cross-site, same-origin` is refused — the verdict depends on ordering rather than on any token being `cross-site`. A header-shaped security control should fail closed on ambiguity: refuse when more than one distinct token is present, or when any token is not in the allow-list. The accompanying test (`github-auth.guard.spec.ts`, 'reads a duplicated or empty Sec-Fetch-Site as its first token') pins the fail-open behaviour as intended, so nothing will catch it later. Not independently exploitable via a browser (the header is forbidden to script), hence low confidence on reachability.

samples.summary: `rawRequest` quotes the raw transport error message unredacted, unlike `fetchOrThrow`, so presigned image-URL query strings / proxy userinfo echoed by undici can reach stderr and CI logs
samples.evidence: `fetchOrThrow` deliberately scrubs the cause through `redactDetail(detail, url)` (errors.ts:167) because "undici and Node echo the request URL verbatim for some failures". The sibling error raised in `rawRequest` interpolates `cause.message` with no such scrubbing: `Request to ${redactUrl(target)} failed: ${cause instanceof Error ? cause.message : String(cause)}` (image-fetcher.ts:665-667). `rawRequest` is the transport for every pinned-proxied hop and every opaque-redirect retry, i.e. exactly the hops whose URLs are attacker/CDN-supplied and routinely carry presigned tokens (`?X-Amz-Signature=…`) or, for the proxy leg, `http://user:pass@proxy:8080`. `docs/design/cli.md` states as a property that "The underlying transport error is scrubbed the same way before it is quoted", which is untrue on this path.

samples.summary: Documented control absent: the OAuth callback still creates/updates the user record before any `state` validation, though the lessons doc added in this change claims the order was fixed and asserted by a test
samples.evidence: `docs/tasks/active/20260803-cli-system-exit-code-lessons.md` (added by this change) states: "Fail-closed belongs before the side effects. The callback created the user account and *then* decided whether the callback was legitimate... state validation now runs first and the test asserts `findOrCreateUser` was never called." In the tree, `githubAuthCallback` calls `this.userService.findOrCreateUser({...})` at auth.controller.ts:117, and the first `state` check is at line 146 (`if (typeof stateToken !== 'string' || !stateToken)`), with the web/CLI cookie binding after it. `GitHubStrategy` installs no passport state store (github.strategy.ts:43-49 — no `store`/`state` option), so nothing validates state before the controller either. Consequence: an unauthenticated request carrying any GitHub-valid code (throttled 10/min) performs a user-table write that the state gate is about to reject, and every `auth.controller.spec.ts` CLI/web-state test mocks `findOrCreateUser` as *called* (lines 195-387), so no test asserts the claimed ordering. Impact is limited (no session is issued, and sign-up is public), but a design-doc/lessons claim that a control exists where it does not is the failure mode those very lessons warn about.
searchedFor: read packages/backend/src/auth/github.strategy.ts for a passport state store

samples.summary: The opaque-redirect fallback re-issues the hop through raw undici, bypassing the injected `opts.fetch` transport entirely
samples.evidence: `issue()` calls `fetchOrThrow(..., fetchImpl)` and then, if `isOpaqueRedirect(res)` (status 0 or type `opaqueredirect`, line 634-636), silently re-issues the same hop with `rawRequest(plan.url, plan.agent, plan.headers)` (line 780), which uses `undiciRequest` directly. Any egress restriction, instrumentation, or allow-listing an embedder/test places on the `fetch` seam is therefore not authoritative: a transport that answers with a network-error/status-0 `Response` (which is what `Response.error()` and several stubs produce) causes the CLI to make a real outbound request through undici instead. The address pin and the gate still apply, so this is a defence-in-depth gap rather than an SSRF, but the `fetch` seam should not be silently escapable.

samples.summary: `isPrivateAddress` misses the IPv4-translated `::ffff:0:0/96` spelling and non-well-known NAT64 prefixes
samples.evidence: The zero-prefix branch only reaches the embedded-IPv4 rules when `words.slice(0,5).every(w => w === 0)` (line 167), i.e. when the `ffff` marker sits in word 5. For `::ffff:0:7f00:1` (RFC 2765 IPv4-translated, `::ffff:0:0/96`) the marker is in word 4, so `words[4] === 0xffff` fails that test and the function returns `false` — a `src` of `http://[::ffff:0:7f00:1]/` is judged public by the gate and pinned to that literal. Likewise only the well-known NAT64 prefix `64:ff9b::/96` is recognised; a site's network-specific NAT64 prefix (RFC 6052 §2.2) is not, so on such a host an IPv6 literal embedding `169.254.169.254` passes. Exploitability is low — mainstream kernels do not route `::ffff:0:x` to the v4 address, and network-specific prefixes are site-dependent — but both are spellings of the addresses this table exists to refuse, and the surrounding tests enumerate every other transition form.

samples.summary: A request with no `Sec-Fetch-Site` is served, so the CLI-start refusal is inert on browsers that do not send the header
samples.evidence: `assertCliStartNotCrossSite` returns early when `parseFetchSite` yields `undefined` (line 173). The comment justifies this with "every browser that can be steered cross-site also sends this", which is not true of Safari before 16.4, Firefox before 90, or legacy Edge/IE — on those, a hostile page's cross-site navigation into `?mode=cli` is indistinguishable from the CLI's own OS-opener start. The tradeoff is deliberate and the confirm-cookie gate still applies, so this is hardening only: the header's absence could at least be logged, or refused for CLI starts that also lack the confirm secret.

samples.summary: `apiKeysBase` interpolates `config.workspace` into the URL path without encoding, while the sibling `id` was just given `encodeURIComponent`
samples.evidence: `private get apiKeysBase()` builds `${server}/workspaces/${this.config.workspace}/api-keys` with the workspace taken verbatim from `--workspace` / `WAFFLEBASE_WORKSPACE` / the YAML config, whereas `revokeApiKey` now correctly encodes its id. A workspace value containing `/` or `..` re-targets the request — and with it the `Authorization: Bearer <api key>` header — at a different path on the configured server (e.g. `--workspace 'x/../../auth/me'`). Same-origin only, and the value is operator-supplied, so impact is small; but the diff added encoding on one interpolation of this URL and not the other, and `base` (line 85) has the same shape.

verdict.reason: Verified in the repo: the pin-drop retry at image-fetcher.ts:793-812 fires on ANY SystemError with code 'NETWORK_ERROR' while plan.pinnedThroughProxy is true, and rawRequest (662-670) converts every transport cause (proxy CONNECT refusal, origin TCP reset, TLS handshake failure, unreachable approved address) into exactly that error/code. A document author picking the image host controls that behaviour, so the fallback IS attacker-triggerable, contradicting the doc comment at 507-513. Line 808 sets the fetcher-scoped pinThroughProxy = false (declared at 735, outside the per-URL closure at 757), so for the rest of the export planHop's !pinThroughProxy branch (536-543) returns a bare makeProxyAgent(proxy) with the original hostname and pinnedThroughProxy:false — the proxy resolves each host itself. assertFetchableImageUrl (327-416) only resolves and approves addresses; its own comment (320-325) says the pin is what makes a rejected address unreachable under rebinding, so with the pin dropped a 0-TTL nameserver can answer the gate publicly and the proxy with a private address, reaching internal resources in the proxy's network and embedding the bytes in the exported document. The one-shot warning (736-749) misattributes the cause and cannot distinguish a document-triggered drop from an environmental one. Real, in-lane SSRF/weakened-control weakening; only precondition is a configured egress proxy (proxyForUrl, 603-620).
